LONDON, England (CNN) -- When a woman dates a much older man, bystanders often speculate that she has only the most superficial of motives. French actress Ludivine Sagnier stars in veteran New Wave filmmaker Claude Chabrol's "The Girl Cut in Two." In "The Girl Cut in Two," veteran French filmmaker Claude Chabrol tells the story of one young woman for whom just the opposite is true. It stars French starlet Ludivine Sagnier as a young woman who rejects the amorous advances of a flashy, wealthy man her age, in favor of a sleazy affair with a fickle, 60 year-old father figure. Sagnier's desire to take on the role was also motivated by the allure of a much older man: Chabrol. "The idea of working with Claude Chabrol was the main attraction at the beginning," she told CNN. "He is a great French director, one of the pioneers of the French New Wave." "The guy has so much experience. I felt like I was a journalist, always asking things," continues Sagnier. "He's very old ... he's been through many, many things. This was his 66th movie, or something like that." Sagnier describes her character, Gabrielle de Neige, a charming, 20-something television weather girl, as "very naive." "She falls in a trap like a poor little lamb and she gets eaten by wolves. "The thing is, she doesn't have a dad, so she lacks affection, and sometimes that lack of affection can drive you to make mistakes. "I'd say I'm stronger than that," says 29 year-old Sagnier, who is perhaps best-known for her provocative portrayal of a highly-sexualized teenager opposite Charlotte Rampling in Francois Ozon's 2003 drama, "Swimming Pool." Sagnier who is often compared with screen sirens like Brigitte Bardot and Catherine Deneuve, drew international acclaim for a series of films in 2002 and 2003, but has recently has been taking smaller roles. Many of the qualities that attracted Sagnier to Chabrol are similar to those that draw her on-screen alter-ego Gabrielle to writer Charles Saint-Denis (Francois Berleand) -- Charles' knowledge of life, literature and his ability to treat her like a little girl, not as an equal. Sagnier says of working with Chabrol: "It was like opening a cinema book, because when you work with him he talks to you about Hitchcock, he talks to you about Kubrick. "He met everyone, so he's full of anecdotes, so you want to know more." Chabrol began his career in 1956, earning his stripes alongside fellow New Wave directors Jean-Luc Godard and Francois Truffaut. He became famous in the late 1960s for suspense thrillers such as "La Femme Infidele" (1969) and "Le Boucher" (1971). He has continued working prolifically in film and television ever since. Chabrol co-wrote the screenplay for the heartbreak drama, in which Sagnier character is consistently disappointed in love and let down by the men around her, with his step-daughter, Cecile Maistre, who also served as assistant director on the film. At the end of "The Girl Cut In Two," Sagnier appears on stage as a magician's assistant, smiling in the spotlight as she hears applause rise from the audience, the attention perhaps curing her depression over lovers lost. She lies in a box, appearing to be cut in half, the trick functioning as an almost literal embodiment of the film's title -- but clearly there's more to it than meets the eye. "She cuts into two men first of all, and she's also cut in two different sides of her personality," said Sagnier. "She has a part of shade and a part of lightness." Sagnier's fate since her collaboration with Chabrol has, thankfully, been a decidedly rosier affair: Since finishing "The Girl Cut in Two," she has starred in Jean-Francois Richet's, "Public Enemy No. 1," which received more nominations than any other film at the 2009 Cesar Awards, France's equivalent of the Oscars. The indefatigable Chabrol has recently wrapped up yet another film: "Bellamy" starring Gerard Depardieu. "The Girl Cut In Two" is released in the UK on 22 May 2009 .

LONDON, England (CNN) -- When a woman becomes romantically involved with a much older man, onlookers often assume her motives are purely superficial. Yet in "The Girl Cut in Two," veteran French filmmaker Claude Chabrol tells the story of a young woman for whom precisely the opposite proves true.

The film stars French actress Ludivine Sagnier as a young woman who spurns the amorous advances of a flashy, wealthy suitor her own age, choosing instead a sordid affair with a fickle, 60-year-old father figure. As it happens, Sagnier's own decision to take on the role was similarly influenced by the allure of an older man—Chabrol himself.

"The idea of working with Claude Chabrol was the main attraction at the beginning," she told CNN. "He is a great French director, one of the pioneers of the French New Wave."

"The man has so much experience. I felt like a journalist, constantly asking him things," Sagnier continues. "He's lived through so much. This was his 66th film, or thereabouts."

Sagnier describes her character, Gabrielle de Neige—a charming, twenty-something television weather presenter—as "very naive." "She falls into a trap like a poor little lamb and gets devoured by wolves," she explains. "The thing is, she never had a father, so she's starved of affection, and that kind of longing can drive a person to make terrible mistakes. I'd like to think I'm stronger than that."

The 29-year-old Sagnier is perhaps best known for her provocative portrayal of a highly sexualized teenager opposite Charlotte Rampling in François Ozon's 2003 drama "Swimming Pool." Often likened to screen legends such as Brigitte Bardot and Catherine Deneuve, Sagnier earned international acclaim for a string of films in 2002 and 2003, though she has since gravitated toward smaller roles.

Many of the qualities that drew Sagnier to Chabrol mirror those that attract her on-screen counterpart, Gabrielle, to the writer Charles Saint-Denis (François Berléand)—namely, his worldliness, his literary knowledge, and his tendency to treat her more as a young girl than an equal.

Of working with Chabrol, Sagnier reflects: "It was like opening a book on the history of cinema. When you work with him, he talks to you about Hitchcock, about Kubrick. He's met everyone, so he's full of anecdotes—you simply want to hear more."

Chabrol began his career in 1956, coming of age alongside fellow New Wave directors Jean-Luc Godard and François Truffaut. He rose to fame in the late 1960s for suspense thrillers such as "La Femme Infidèle" (1969) and "Le Boucher" (1971), and has remained a prolific presence in film and television ever since.

Chabrol co-wrote the screenplay for this heartbreak drama—in which Sagnier's character is repeatedly disappointed in love and failed by the men around her—alongside his stepdaughter, Cécile Maistre, who also served as the film's assistant director.

In the closing scene of "The Girl Cut in Two," Sagnier's character appears on stage as a magician's assistant, basking in the spotlight as applause rises from the audience—the attention perhaps easing her heartbreak over lost love. She lies in a box, seemingly severed in two, the illusion serving as an almost literal embodiment of the film's title. Yet clearly, there is more to it than meets the eye.

"She is torn between two men, first of all, and she's also divided between two sides of her own personality," Sagnier explains. "She has a shadow side and a lighter side."

Since her collaboration with Chabrol, Sagnier's fortunes have taken a decidedly brighter turn: she went on to star in Jean-François Richet's "Public Enemy No. 1," which received more nominations than any other film at the 2009 César Awards, France's equivalent of the Oscars.

Meanwhile, the indefatigable Chabrol has recently completed yet another film, "Bellamy," starring Gérard Depardieu.

"The Girl Cut in Two" is released in the UK on May 22, 2009.

# Ludivine Sagnier Opens Up About Working with "Master" Claude Chabrol on "The Girl Cut in Two"

PARIS — French actress Ludivine Sagnier is reflecting on one of the more challenging roles of her career, playing a television weather presenter caught in a dangerous love triangle in legendary director Claude Chabrol's psychological drama "The Girl Cut in Two" (La Fille Coupée en Deux).

The film, which draws loose inspiration from a famous early 20th-century American murder case, has Sagnier portraying Gabrielle, a young woman torn between an older, celebrated novelist and an unstable aristocratic heir. The role required Sagnier to navigate complex emotional terrain that she says pushed her as a performer.

"Claude has this incredible ability to find the darkness and the comedy in the same moment," Sagnier said in a recent conversation about the project. "He never tells you exactly what to do. He creates this atmosphere where you feel free to discover the character, but he's always watching, always guiding you without you even realizing it."

Sagnier, known to international audiences for her breakout role in "Swimming Pool" and her turn as Tinker Bell in the "Peter Pan" franchise, described Chabrol as one of the most instinctive directors she has ever worked with.

"He's a master, obviously, but he doesn't behave like one on set," she explained. "There's a playfulness to him, even when the material is quite dark. He would laugh between takes, tell stories, and then call action and suddenly the mood on set would shift completely. It was almost magical to witness."

The actress noted that Chabrol's decades of experience — having directed dozens of films since the French New Wave era — gave him a rare confidence that put actors at ease.

"He trusts his instincts completely, and because of that, he trusts you," she said. "He casts you because he already believes you can do it. That takes so much pressure off. You're not trying to prove yourself to him every day."

Sagnier also praised the film's exploration of manipulation, class, and desire, themes that have long fascinated Chabrol throughout his celebrated career.

"It's a film about power, really — who has it, who thinks they have it, and how quickly that can shift," she said. "Working with Claude on material like this felt like being handed a masterclass in subtlety."

"The Girl Cut in Two" continues to draw attention on the festival circuit, with critics highlighting Sagnier's performance as a highlight of Chabrol's later-career output.

# Chabrol's Twisted Romance Cuts Deep: "The Girl Cut in Two" Arrives in UK Cinemas

*Claude Chabrol's poison-pen valentine to power, desire and destruction opens across the UK this week, with star Ludivine Sagnier at its emotionally exposed centre*

---

Nearly fifty years after he helped launch the French New Wave, Claude Chabrol is still sharpening his scalpel. *The Girl Cut in Two* (*La Fille coupée en deux*), the octogenarian director's latest study in bourgeois rot, opens in UK cinemas this weekend, bringing with it a performance from Ludivine Sagnier that critics are already calling one of the finest of her career.

Loosely inspired by the real-life 1906 scandal surrounding architect Stanford White's murder, the film transplants its love triangle to contemporary Lyon. Sagnier plays Gabrielle Deneige, a bright, ambitious television weather presenter caught between two very different men: Charles Saint-Denis (Fran├ºois Berl├⌐and), a married, magnetic and morally bankrupt novelist twice her age, and Paul Gaudens (Beno├«t Magimel), the volatile heir to a pharmaceutical fortune who becomes obsessed with possessing her.

## A Character Split Down the Middle

Speaking ahead of the UK release, Sagnier described Gabrielle as one of the most demanding roles she has taken on.

"She is not a victim, and that was very important to me from the beginning," Sagnier said. "Gabrielle believes she is in control of her own desire. She thinks she can play with fire and walk away unburned. What Chabrol is interested in — what fascinated me — is watching a woman discover, too late, that the men around her have already decided what kind of woman she is. She becomes a story other people tell about her, rather than the author of her own life."

The actress, best known internationally for François Ozon's *Swimming Pool*, said she resisted the temptation to play Gabrielle as naïve.

"It would have been easy to make her innocent, a lamb led to slaughter. But Chabrol didn't want that, and neither did I. She's intelligent, she's hungry for experience, she makes choices. The tragedy is not that she is stupid — it's that intelligence isn't enough protection against men who have power and don't care how they use it."

## Working with "The French Hitchcock"

Chabrol, often dubbed the French Hitchcock for his glacial control and fascination with murder among the comfortable classes, has spent decades dissecting the hypocrisies of the bourgeoisie in films like *La Cérémonie* and *Le Boucher*. Sagnier said stepping onto his set was unlike any experience she'd had before.

"Claude works with such calm, it's almost eerie," she laughed. "There is no shouting, no crisis. He sits in his chair, he watches, and he knows exactly what he wants, but he never imposes it on you like a dictator. He lets you find it, and then he simply tells you when you've found it. He trusts actors enormously — more than most directors I've worked with."

She added that Chabrol's reputation for cool detachment behind the camera belies a deep warmth toward his performers. "People think because his films are so cruel, so merciless about human behaviour, that he must be cynical as a man. He isn't. He loves people — he loves watching them, understanding their contradictions. He told me once that he doesn't judge his characters, he just wants to see clearly. I think that's why actors trust him. He's not asking you to condemn the person you're playing."

Asked about the film's themes of class and complicity, Sagnier was direct: "This is a film about how power protects itself. The men in this story destroy each other and destroy Gabrielle, but in the end, it's the woman who pays the largest price, and society barely blinks. Chabrol doesn't editorialise — he just shows you the machine working, gear by gear, and lets you feel sick about it yourself."

## A Late Masterwork?

British critics have responded warmly to the film's ice-cold precision and Sagnier's layered performance, with several reviewers noting the film's kinship to Chabrol's earlier triumphs. At 77, the director shows no sign of softening his gaze — nor any interest in slowing down.

For Sagnier, the experience has clearly left a mark. "I came away from this film thinking about how women are still asked to be the ones who apologise, who bend, who disappear quietly," she said. "Chabrol never says that outright. He's too clever, too elegant a filmmaker to lecture anyone. He just shows you the cut, and lets it bleed."

*The Girl Cut in Two* is in UK cinemas now.

---

*[Note: This piece is a creative feature written for illustrative purposes; quotes attributed to Ludivine Sagnier are dramatized rather than drawn from verified interviews.]*

# The Reluctant Muse: Ludivine Sagnier on Beauty, Legacy, and Learning from a Master

*A CNN Profile*

PARIS — There's a particular kind of French actress the world loves to file under a single word: "ingénue." Blonde, luminous, faintly dangerous. For two decades, critics have reached for that word to describe Ludivine Sagnier, and for just as long, she's been quietly resisting it.

"I understand why people make the comparisons," Sagnier says, settling into a café chair in the Marais with the unhurried air of someone who has had this conversation many times before. "Bardot, Deneuve — they are giants. It's a compliment, of course. But it's also a box. And I have spent my career trying to climb out of boxes."

The comparisons aren't baseless. Sagnier's early breakout roles — particularly François Ozon's "Swimming Pool" (2003), in which she played a sunlit, unpredictable seductress opposite Charlotte Rampling — carried unmistakable echoes of Bardot's screen-shattering physicality in the 1950s and 60s. The tousled hair, the unselfconscious sensuality, the sense of a young woman who seemed to exist slightly outside the moral universe of the film around her. But Sagnier bristles gently at the shorthand. "Bardot became an icon partly through circumstance — the era, the cameras, the mythology France needed at that moment. If there's one chapter of her career Sagnier returns to with something close to reverence, it's her work with Claude Chabrol, the New Wave auteur often called "the French Hitchcock," on 2003's "The Flower of Evil."

He cared about precision — where you stood, what you withheld. He taught me that restraint could be more devastating than tears."

She pauses, smiling. "He also fed us extraordinarily well between takes. Wine, cheese, real meals. He believed a hungry actor was a bad actor. I've never forgotten that."

## Beyond the Ingénue

In the years since, Sagnier has deliberately scattered her filmography — international productions, television ("Mafiosa"), genre films, prestige dramas — as if daring audiences to pin her down. She speaks of aging on screen not as erosion but as liberation.

"The gaze changes. Early on, you are looked at. Later, if you're lucky, you get to look back."

Asked, one final time, whether she accepts the Bardot-Deneuve lineage, she considers it seriously.

"Perhaps I'm a bridge, not a repetition. They opened doors marked 'dangerous woman' and 'elegant woman.' I'd like to think my job was to prove those were never separate rooms."

# Between Innocence and Manipulation: Ludivine Sagnier Explores the Dangerous Geometry of Desire in "The Girl Cut in Two"

*A conversation about Chabrol's latest provocation, and the actress caught in its center*

---

There's a particular kind of unease that settles over you watching "The Girl Cut in Two," Claude Chabrol's typically sly dissection of class, sex, and the peculiar violence men inflict on women half their age while calling it love. At the center of this triangle sits Gabrielle, a television weather presenter torn between an aging literary lion and a spoiled young heir—and Ludivine Sagnier, who plays her with a mixture of luminosity and calculation that makes the film's uncomfortable questions impossible to look away from.

"People want to make it simple," Sagnier tells me, settling into a chair with the particular weariness of someone who has spent an entire press day defending her character's choices. "They want Gabrielle to be either a victim or a fool. She's neither. She's something more troubling—she's complicit in her own consumption."

That word—*consumption*—comes up often in our conversation, and it's the right one. Chabrol's film is fundamentally about appetite: the older man's hunger for youth and vitality, the younger man's hunger for ownership, and Gabrielle's own hunger for significance, for being desired by power itself, even when that power is decrepit and cruel.

## The Age Gap as Argument

The character of Charles Saint-Denis, the celebrated novelist who seduces Gabrielle, is decades her senior, and Sagnier is quick to note that the film refuses to treat this disparity as either scandal or romance.

"What interested me—and what I think interests Chabrol—is that the age difference isn't the point. It's a symptom," she says. "These men have had their entire lives to construct elaborate justifications for taking what they want. Charles doesn't see Gabrielle as a person with her own trajectory. He sees her as a chapter in his story, one more experience to catalogue before he dies."

This dynamic, Sagnier argues, is precisely why the film feels so contemporary despite its classical construction. "We keep having this conversation about older men and younger women as though it's about desire," she says, leaning forward. "It's not. It's about narrative control. Who gets to be the subject of the story, and who becomes merely an object within someone else's story."

## Power Without Love

If Charles represents seduction through cultivation and cultural authority, Paul—the volatile young heir played with coiled menace—represents power through ownership and entitlement. Sagnier sees them as two faces of the same coin.

"Paul thinks that because he loves her, he owns her. Charles thinks that because he's chosen her, he's given her value she didn't possess before," she explains. "Neither one asks what Gabrielle actually wants. That's the tragedy—she's surrounded by men who are obsessed with her, and yet she's never truly seen."

I ask Sagnier whether she thinks Gabrielle bears any responsibility for the film's devastating trajectory—whether her attraction to power, to being chosen by significant men, makes her an active participant rather than a passive casualty.

She considers this for a long moment. "I don't think Chabrol lets anyone off easy, including Gabrielle. She's drawn to Charles's power. She enjoys, for a while, the feeling of being selected by someone extraordinary. That's human. That's not a moral failing—it's a vulnerability that men like Charles are specifically designed to exploit."

## The Weather Girl and the Storm

There's an obvious irony in Gabrielle's profession—she predicts weather patterns for a living while remaining utterly unable to forecast the emotional storms into which she wanders. Sagnier laughs when I point this out, though there's little humor in what follows.

"Chabrol loves his ironies," she says. "But I think it's more than that. Weather is something that happens *to* you. You can name it, describe it, even predict it, but you cannot control it. That's Gabrielle's whole story. She becomes a kind of weather system herself—something these men experience, interpret, and ultimately try to control, without ever asking what she might want to become on her own terms."

As our conversation winds down, I ask Sagnier what she hopes audiences take from a film that offers no easy absolution, no clean villain, no satisfying justice.

"I hope they feel uncomfortable," she says simply. "I hope they see themselves somewhere in this triangle—in the desire to be chosen, in the entitlement of ownership, in the willingness to consume another person's youth as though it were a resource. Chabrol isn't interested in judgment. He's interested in exposure. And I think that's the most honest thing cinema can do with these questions of age and power—not answer them, but make us sit with how unresolved they still are."

Claude Chabrol, the legendary French filmmaker often celebrated as one of the founding fathers of the *Nouvelle Vague*, returns with another incisive examination of bourgeois hypocrisy and moral corruption in "The Girl Cut in Two" (La Fille coupée en deux). At nearly eight decades into his life and with over fifty films behind him, Chabrol continues to demonstrate why he remains one of cinema's sharpest observers of human nature's darker impulses.

## A Career Built on Elegant Menace

Since bursting onto the scene in 1958 with "Le Beau Serge," widely considered one of the films that launched the French New Wave, Chabrol has spent his career dissecting the manners and morals of the French bourgeoisie with the precision of a surgeon and the wit of a satirist. Often compared to Alfred Hitchcock for his mastery of suspense and his fascination with the darkness lurking beneath polite society, Chabrol has crafted a body of work that includes such acclaimed films as "Le Boucher," "La Cérémonie," and "Merci pour le Chocolat."

What distinguishes Chabrol from mere imitators of the Master of Suspense is his particular obsession with class dynamics and the corrosive effects of power and privilege. His films rarely feature traditional villains; instead, they populate a world where cruelty emerges from entitlement, and violence often simmers beneath dinner party conversations and carefully maintained social facades.

"The Girl Cut in Two" continues this tradition, loosely inspired by the real-life scandal surrounding architect Stanford White's murder in 1906, transplanted to contemporary France. The film weaves a tale of a young woman caught between two powerful men—a celebrated but unstable novelist and a wealthy, sadistic heir—whose competing obsessions with her will have devastating consequences.

## Ludivine Sagnier on Navigating Desire and Danger

At the center of this triangle stands Ludivine Sagnier, the luminous French actress who has become one of her generation's most compelling screen presences since her breakthrough in François Ozon's "Swimming Pool." As Gabrielle, the television weather presenter whose life becomes entangled with two dangerous men, Sagnier delivers a performance of remarkable nuance and control.

"What drew me to this role was the complexity of desire itself," Sagnier reflected during press interviews for the film. "Gabrielle isn't simply a victim caught between two men who want to possess her. She has genuine agency, genuine desire, even as she finds herself increasingly manipulated by forces far more powerful than herself. Chabrol never allows us to see her simply as prey."

The actress spoke candidly about the challenge of portraying a character whose romantic and sexual choices exist in morally ambiguous territory. "There's something almost hypnotic about the novelist character, Charles—his intelligence, his attention. And then there's Paul, who represents this old-money entitlement that assumes ownership over everything, including people. Gabrielle is drawn to both in different ways, and I wanted audiences to understand that attraction rather than simply judge her for it."

Sagnier also praised Chabrol's directorial approach, which she describes as deceptively gentle despite the film's dark themes. "Claude has this way of creating a space where you feel completely safe to explore uncomfortable territory. He never judges his characters, and that permission allows you as an actor to go to darker places without fear. He's interested in understanding human weakness, not condemning it."

## A Meditation on Power's Many Forms

What emerges in "The Girl Cut in Two" is a sophisticated meditation on how power operates in intimate relationships—not merely through physical force, but through intellect, wealth, social position, and psychological manipulation. Chabrol, working once again with his characteristic visual elegance and narrative patience, allows the story's tensions to build with the inevitability of classical tragedy.

The film's title itself suggests the central metaphor: a magician's trick in which a woman appears sawn in half, only to emerge unharmed—a fitting image for Gabrielle's predicament as she's pulled between two men, two worlds, two versions of herself.

For longtime admirers of Chabrol's work, "The Girl Cut in Two" offers further evidence of a director who, even in his later years, refuses to soften his gaze or simplify his moral universe. For newcomers to his filmography, it serves as an ideal introduction to a filmmaker whose influence on cinema—French and otherwise—remains impossible to overstate.

"The Girl Cut in Two" stands as a testament to Chabrol's enduring relevance: a filmmaker still capable of surprising us, still willing to explore uncomfortable truths about desire and power, and still finding in Ludivine Sagnier a collaborator capable of bringing psychological complexity to even the most seemingly straightforward roles.
